newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil prices end firm on tensions with Iran.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil prices end firm on tensions with Iran.

text.p: NYMEX oil prices ended with healthy gains Monday on a report linking Iran, the third largest oil exporter in the world, to the 1996 bombing of U.S. barracks in Saudi Arabia.
The report comes at time when diplomatic tensions are already high between the West and Iran.

"The report linking Iran to the bombing set the stage for further gains today when tensions were already mounting since Thursday with the Germany-Iran situation," said Richard Redash, analyst with Prudential Securities in New York.
May crude ended up 37 cents at $19.90 a barrel.

Spot crude rose to a session high of $20.01, the first time spot crude rose above $20.00 since April 2. May gasoline settled 1.08 cents higher at 61.96 cents a gallon while May heating oil ended up 0.80 cent at 54.67 cents gallon.

The Washington Post on Sunday reported that U.S. and Saudi intelligence authorities had linked a senior Iranian government official to a group suspected of the 1996 bombing of the Khobar U.S. military compound in Saudi Arabia.

In Tehran, meanwhile, several hundred students clashed with police outside the German embassy during a demonstration against last week's Berlin court ruling that Iran ordered the killing of dissidents.

Analysts said the market is concerned that if tensions between the West and Iran continue to escalate, oil business from Iran could end up being curtailed down the road through sanctions by European countries, tighening supply.
The United States already prohibits Iranian oil imports.

Crude prices were also supported by deep-draft shipping traffic remaining restricted to one-way at a time on Monday along a section of the Houston Ship Channel where a barge lost a load of large tanks last week.
Dealers mostly shrugged off the ship channel troubles as the slowed oil shipments were seen only temporary.
More importantly, shipping has returned to near-normal along the waterway linking the Port of Houston and refinery row to the Gulf of Mexico, Ship Channel officials said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
